usage: Polite; the all-purpose soft 'no' when offered something
반말, to a friend turning down an offer
Formal 합쇼체, to a clerk, officer, or in business
Add 저는 to make clear YOU are declining, not commenting on the thing
examples: 괜찮아요.
No thanks, I'm fine.
Said with a small hand wave when someone offers more food or a bag
봉투 드릴까요? — 아, 괜찮아요.
Shall I give you a bag? — Oh, I'm okay.
The everyday cashier exchange; 괜찮아요 declines the bag
좀 더 드세요. — 아니에요, 많이 먹었어요. 괜찮아요.
Have some more. — No really, I've eaten a lot. I'm fine.
Refusing a second helping; pair with a reason so it doesn't sound curt
nuance: 괜찮아요 literally means 'it's okay/fine', but in an offer situation it is the No.1 polite way to say 'no thank you' — you are signalling 'I'm fine as I am, so I don't need it.' Koreans use it constantly to refuse a plastic bag, a refill, more food, help, or a sample. Register: 괜찮아요 is polite-neutral for staff and acquaintances; drop to 괜찮아 with friends, lift to 괜찮습니다 in formal settings. The big trap for English speakers is that 괜찮아요 is ALSO the answer to 'how are you?' and to 'is this okay?', so context decides whether it means 'I'm well', 'that's fine', or 'no thanks' — when it follows an offer, it's a refusal. The classic mistake is answering an offer with a literal 아니요 ('no') alone, which sounds blunt and a bit cold; 괜찮아요 is the gentle, face-saving 'no'. Also note: when a waiter asks 'do you want a bag/receipt?', 괜찮아요 = 'no', whereas 네 = 'yes' — beginners sometimes say 네 meaning 'I heard you' and accidentally accept. Reinforce the refusal with a hand gesture or 아니에요 so there's no doubt.

usage: Polite; a firmer, warmer double 'no thanks'
Formal 합쇼체, to staff or in business
Add 진짜 ('really') to insist when they keep offering
examples: 아니에요, 괜찮아요.
No really, I'm fine.
Said while gently pushing back when someone insists
이거 가져가세요. — 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 마음만 받을게요.
Take this. — No really, I'm fine. I appreciate the thought.
마음만 받을게요 ('I'll just take the thought') softens the refusal
제가 도와드릴게요. — 아, 아니에요, 괜찮아요. 혼자 할 수 있어요.
Let me help you. — Oh no, it's fine. I can do it alone.
Declining offered help while reassuring them
nuance: 아니에요, 괜찮아요 stacks 아니에요 ('it's not so / no') in front of 괜찮아요 to make a refusal that is both clear and warm — the 아니에요 firmly turns down the offer while 괜찮아요 reassures 'I'm okay, don't worry about me.' Koreans typically offer two or three times out of politeness, so you often need this stronger version when one 괜찮아요 isn't taken. The key learner point is that 아니에요 (the soft 'it's not / no') is the natural refusal particle here, NOT 아니요 — though both exist, 아니에요 flows better before 괜찮아요 and sounds gentler. A trap: do NOT decline a gift or kindness with a cold single 싫어요 ('I don't like/want it'), which is for genuine dislike and sounds harsh; 싫어요 to a host's food can be offensive. english: Right now isn't great for me
usage: Polite; vague soft refusal without giving a reason
Formal, to a senior or in business
Swap 지금은 for 그건 to call a specific thing awkward
examples: 지금은 좀 그래요.
Now isn't really a good time.
Declining an invite or request without spelling out why
오늘 같이 술 한잔 어때요? — 아, 오늘은 좀 그래요. 다음에요.
How about a drink today? — Ah, today's not great for me. Another time.
Softly declining tonight while leaving the door open with 다음에요
이 가격에 어떠세요? — 음… 그건 좀 그런데요.
How about this price? — Hmm… that's a bit much.
Using 그건 좀 그런데요 to push back on an offer without flat rejection
nuance: 좀 그래요 is one of the most Korean phrases there is: literally '(it's) a bit like that', it deliberately leaves the negative UNSAID. 그렇다 ('to be so/like that') stands in for an awkward, uncomfortable, or undesirable quality the speaker won't name, and 좀 ('a bit') softens it further — so the whole thing means 'it's kind of… not ideal' without you ever having to say why. This indirectness is the point: it declines or expresses reluctance while saving everyone's face. Register: polite 좀 그래요, casual 좀 그래, formal 좀 그렇습니다 / 좀 그런데요. The dividing line from 안 돼요 ('it's not possible / no') is bluntness — 안 돼요 is a hard no, while 좀 그래요 is a soft, deniable 'eh, not really.' The huge English-speaker trap is treating 그래요 as 'yes, that's right' (its other meaning, as agreement) — but 좀 그래요 with a hesitant tone is the OPPOSITE: a polite refusal. Another error is demanding or expecting a reason; Korean culture accepts 좀 그래요 as a complete, reason-free decline, and pressing 'why?' (왜요?) can feel pushy. Deliver it with a slight trailing tone and maybe 좀 그런데요 to invite the other person to back off gracefully.

usage: Polite; declines now but promises later
Formal 합쇼체, to a senior or at work
Short form; just 'next time' as a gentle pass
examples: 다음에 할게요.
I'll do it next time.
Politely passing on something offered now
같이 점심 어때요? — 오늘은 약속이 있어서, 다음에 할게요.
Lunch together? — I have plans today, so let's do it next time.
Give a light reason, then defer with 다음에 할게요
멤버십 가입하시겠어요? — 아, 다음에 할게요. 오늘은 그냥 살게요.
Would you like to sign up for membership? — Ah, maybe next time. I'll just buy it today.

nuance: 다음에 할게요 is 다음에 ('next time') + 할게요 (the -ㄹ게요 promise/intention form of 하다 'to do'), meaning 'I'll do it next time' — a soft refusal that declines the present offer while leaving the relationship warm by implying you'll come back to it. The -ㄹ게요 ending is key: it frames the deferral as YOUR own intention/promise, which feels considerate. Often it's just politeness, not a real commitment — both sides understand 다음에 ('next time') may never come, like the English 'maybe some other time.' Register: 다음에 할게요 polite, 다음에 할게 casual, 다음에 하겠습니다 formal. The dividing line from 안 할게요 ('I won't do it') is that 안 할게요 closes the door, while 다음에 할게요 keeps it ajar — much softer for declining invitations, sign-ups, or offers. The English-speaker trap is using 다음에 합시다 ('let's do it next time') when YOU are the one declining: 합시다 ('let's') is a suggestion/command to the group and can sound like you're scheduling them, whereas 할게요 humbly states your own choice. Another error is over-promising — Koreans read 다음에 할게요 as a polite brush-off, so don't be hurt if a 다음에 plan never materializes, and don't feel you broke a promise if yours doesn't either.

Confusing 할게요 with 하고 싶어요.
하고 싶어요 means 'I want to do it'. To politely defer doing it now, say 다음에 할게요. Saying 다음에 하고 싶어요 sounds like expressing a wish, not declining the present offer.

usage: Polite; declines an outing but stays friendly
반말, to a friend inviting you out
Formal, to a senior or boss
다음 기회에 ('next opportunity') sounds a touch warmer/sincerer
examples: 다음에 갈게요.
I'll go next time.
Turning down an invitation to go somewhere together
회식 오실 거죠? — 오늘은 몸이 안 좋아서, 다음에 갈게요.
You're coming to the work dinner, right? — I'm not feeling well today, so I'll go next time.
Declining a 회식 (company dinner) with a health reason
노래방 갈래요? — 저는 먼저 갈게요. 다음에 같이 가요.
Wanna go to noraebang? — I'll head off first. Let's go together next time.
Bowing out now while proposing a real future plan with 다음에 같이 가요
nuance: 다음에 갈게요 is 다음에 ('next time') + 갈게요 (-ㄹ게요 form of 가다 'to go'), the standard soft way to decline an invitation to go somewhere — a meal, a 회식 (work dinner), a 노래방 trip — while signalling goodwill ('I'll join next time'). Like 다음에 할게요, it is often a courteous brush-off rather than a firm plan, especially for the near-obligatory Korean 회식 culture where bowing out gracefully matters. Register: 갈게요 polite, 갈게 casual, 가겠습니다 formal. A warmer, more sincere upgrade is 다음 기회에 꼭 갈게요 ('I'll definitely go next chance'), where 꼭 ('for sure') signals you really mean it. Another error is treating a refused 회식 lightly in a strict workplace; even with 다음에 갈게요, add a real reason (몸이 안 좋아서, 선약이 있어서) to soften it.

Declining a 회식 with a bare 안 갈게요 and no reason.
In many Korean workplaces a flat refusal sounds cold. Soften with a reason plus 다음에 갈게요: 오늘은 선약이 있어서 다음에 갈게요.
Promising 다음에 꼭 갈게요 you don't mean.
꼭 ('definitely') raises the commitment. If it's really just a polite pass, plain 다음에 갈게요 is enough; over-promising with 꼭 can create expectations.

english: Today won't work for me, I think
usage: Formal, swapping in 어렵다 for the workplace
힘들다 ('to be hard') variant, very common spoken hedge
examples: 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요.
I don't think today will work.
Turning down a same-day plan gently
이따 잠깐 볼 수 있어요? — 죄송한데 오늘은 안 될 것 같아요.
Can we meet briefly later? — Sorry, but today probably won't work.
죄송한데 ('sorry, but') + the hedge makes a courteous refusal
내일까지 끝낼 수 있을까요? — 음, 솔직히 내일까지는 힘들 것 같아요.
Could you finish it by tomorrow? — Hmm, honestly by tomorrow seems tough.
Hedging on a deadline you can't meet without a flat 'no'

That -것 같다 is the single most important softening tool in Korean: by framing the 'no' as your tentative impression rather than a hard fact, you avoid sounding blunt or final. 오늘은 ('as for today', with the topic particle 은 implying contrast) hints 'maybe another day', which softens further. Register: 안 될 것 같아요 polite, 안 될 것 같아 casual, 어려울/안 될 것 같습니다 formal. Common swap-ins are 어렵다 ('to be difficult') and 힘들다 ('to be hard/tough') — 어려울 것 같아요 and 힘들 것 같아요 are slightly more graceful than the plain 안 되다. The topic 은 in 오늘은 implies contrast ('today specifically'), hinting another day is fine. Dropping it (오늘 안 될 것 같아요) is okay but loses that soft, door-open feeling.

usage: Polite; non-committal, often a soft no
Formal 합쇼체, business or to a senior
Let me think a bit more
Add 좀 더 ('a bit more') to ask for time / hedge harder
examples: 생각해 볼게요.
I'll think about it.
Non-committal reply to an offer or a sales pitch
이 제품 어떠세요? — 음, 생각해 볼게요. 좀 둘러보고 올게요.
How about this product? — Hmm, I'll think about it. Let me look around.
Politely escaping a pushy salesperson
주말에 등산 같이 갈래요? — 오, 좋은데… 생각해 볼게요. 일정 보고 연락드릴게요.
Want to hike this weekend? — Oh, sounds good… I'll think about it. I'll check my schedule and let you know.
Buying time on an invite while leaving it genuinely open
nuance: 생각해 볼게요 is 생각하다 ('to think') + -아/어 보다 ('to try doing') + -ㄹ게요 (intention), literally 'I'll try thinking about it' — i.e. 'I'll consider it.' The -어 보다 ('give it a try') makes it tentative, and like in English, 'I'll think about it' is frequently a polite, face-saving NO, especially toward salespeople and pushy invitations. The dividing line from 안 살게요 / 안 할게요 ('I won't buy/do it') is that those are clear refusals, while 생각해 볼게요 declines softly and defers, avoiding an awkward direct 'no.' To buy time more explicitly, add 좀 더 ('a bit more') or follow with 둘러보고 올게요 ('I'll look around and come back'), the classic line for leaving a shop without buying.

english: It feels like too much / It makes me uncomfortable
usage: It's a bit much for me
Polite; declining because it feels like too big a favor/gift
Formal, in business or to a senior
Flip side: what you say to relieve someone else's pressure
examples: 좀 부담스러워요.
It feels like a bit much.
Declining an over-generous gift or gesture
이거 받으세요. — 아유, 이렇게까지… 좀 부담스러워요.
Please take this. — Oh, you didn't have to… this is a bit much.
이렇게까지 ('to go this far') + 부담스러워요 to refuse an extravagant gift
제가 다 계산할게요. — 아니에요, 그러면 제가 너무 부담스러워요. 더치페이해요.

The English-speaker trap is mistranslating 부담 as merely 'pressure/stress' and missing the indebtedness nuance, or using 스트레스 받아요 ('I'm stressed'), which is about general stress, not the specific 'this is too much kindness' feeling. usage: Polite; graciously refuses a gift while honoring the giver
I shall accept your kind thought
Just the thought is more than enough

I'll just accept the thought.
Refusing a gift kindly without seeming ungrateful
이거 작은 거예요, 받으세요. — 아유, 마음만 받을게요. 정말 감사해요.
It's just a small thing, please take it. — Oh, I'll just accept the thought. Thank you so much.

The dividing line from a flat 안 받을게요 ('I won't take it') is warmth — 안 받을게요 can sound like rejecting the person, while 마음만 받을게요 explicitly cherishes their thought. usage: Polite; a respectable reason to decline, trailing off
I have a prior engagement, so it'll be difficult
Formal, completing the sentence for the workplace

I have prior plans, so…
Declining an invite by citing an existing commitment
오늘 저녁에 시간 돼요? — 아, 죄송해요. 오늘은 선약이 있어서요.
Free this evening? — Ah, I'm sorry. I already have plans today.
The polite trailing -서요 lets you decline without a blunt full stop
회식 참석 가능하세요? — 죄송합니다. 그날은 선약이 있어서 참석이 어려울 것 같습니다.
Can you attend the work dinner? — I'm sorry. I have a prior engagement that day, so attending will be difficult.
Formal workplace refusal stacking 선약 + 어려울 것 같다

english: If it's okay with you, maybe next time
usage: If you don't mind, next time
Polite; defers using honorific 시 to respect the other person
반말/plain, to a friend or peer
If you're okay with it, I'll do it next chance
If you happen to be okay with it
혹시 ('by any chance') makes it extra tentative
examples: 괜찮으시면 다음에 할게요.
If it's okay with you, let's do it next time.
Deferring respectfully to someone senior
오늘 한잔 어떠세요? — 아, 부장님, 괜찮으시면 다음에 모실게요. 오늘은 몸이 좀…
How about a drink today? — Ah, sir, if you don't mind, I'll treat you next time. Today I'm a bit…
Declining a senior's invite with 모시다 (humble 'serve/accompany')
지금 회의 가능할까요? — 죄송한데, 괜찮으시면 30분 뒤에 해도 될까요?
Could we meet now? — Sorry, but if it's okay with you, could we do it in 30 minutes?

nuance: 괜찮으시면 다음에 is 괜찮다 ('to be okay') + the honorific infix -시- + the conditional -면 ('if'), so 괜찮으시면 = 'if YOU (respectfully) are okay with it', followed by 다음에 ('next time'). It declines or postpones while explicitly handing the decision to the other person's comfort — the honorific 시 elevates THEM, making this ideal for declining a senior, boss, or anyone you must respect. The conditional 'if you're okay' frame is deeply polite because it asks permission to defer rather than just announcing it. Register: 괜찮으시면 (honorific, to superiors), 괜찮으면 (plain, to peers/friends). Pair it with humble verbs toward seniors: 모실게요 ('I'll accompany/treat you', humble) or 하겠습니다. Add 혹시 ('by any chance') up front for maximum tentativeness. This frame also works to soften REQUESTS, not just refusals ('if you're okay with it, could we…?').

english: That'll probably be a bit difficult
usage: That'll be a bit hard, I think
그건 제가 좀 곤란할 것 같아요
That would put me in a tough spot
곤란하다 ('to be in a bind') variant for an awkward ask
examples: 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요.
That'll be a bit difficult, I think.
Declining a specific request without a flat 'no'
주말에도 좀 나와 줄 수 있어요? — 아… 그건 좀 어려울 것 같아요. 주말엔 가족이랑 약속이 있어서요.
Could you come in on weekends too? — Ah… that'll be a bit difficult. I have family plans on weekends.
Refusing extra work with a hedge plus a reason
가격 좀 더 깎아 주실 수 있어요? — 죄송한데 그건 좀 어려울 것 같습니다. 이미 많이 빼 드린 거예요.
Could you discount it a bit more? — Sorry, but that'll be difficult. I've already taken a lot off.

Here 어렵다 ('difficult') is a euphemism for 'impossible / no' — Koreans rarely say a blunt 안 돼요 ('can't') to a request when they can say 'that would be difficult', which softens the rejection while still being clearly negative. The -것 같다 hedge and the cushioning 좀 add deniability and politeness. Register: 어려울 것 같아요 polite, 어려울 것 같아 casual, 어려울 것 같습니다 formal. The English-speaker trap is taking 어렵다 literally as 'difficult but possible with effort' and then pushing harder ('but could you try?'); in refusal context it means 'no', so pressing is impolite. A near-synonym is 곤란하다 ('to be in an awkward bind'), used when the ask would personally embarrass or trouble you.

usage: Polite; soft refusal with conjecture 겠 + trailing 는데요

That'd be tough, I'm afraid.
Reacting to a request you can't grant, trailing off
내일까지 가능할까요? — 음, 내일까지는 좀 어렵겠는데요. 모레는 어떠세요?

Polite; cushions a refusal with gratitude first

I really appreciate the thought, but…

Sorry, but it puts me in a tough spot.

structuredNuance.t: 됐어요 as a refusal means 'that's enough / I'm good / never mind, don't bother.' It is a FIRMER, more final 'no thanks' than 괜찮아요: you use it to wave something off decisively, often after a first soft refusal didn't land, or to stop someone from doing more for you. Tone is everything: said warmly it's a friendly 'I'm all set', but said flatly or sharply — especially bare 됐어 in 반말 — it can sound curt, dismissive, or even annoyed ('forget it / drop it'), so it carries risk upward. Avoid the curt bare 됐어 toward anyone you must respect.

The dividing line from 괜찮아요 is firmness and finality: 괜찮아요 gently declines and invites no friction, while 됐어요 closes the matter and can imply mild impatience if overdone — so default to 괜찮아요 with strangers/seniors and reserve 됐어요 for when you need to be more definite.
됐어요 comes from 되다 ('to be done/enough') in the past — literally 'it's become (enough)'.
Register: 됐어요 polite-casual, 됐습니다 formal, 됐어 casual/blunt.

The trap is using 됐어요 too readily as a neutral 'no thanks' and accidentally sounding short with a server or elder; soften it with 아니요 or 괜찮아요 in front (아니요, 됐어요 / 괜찮아요, 됐어요). Another error is confusing the refusal 됐어요 with the affirmative 됐어요/됐다 meaning 'it worked! / it's done!' (e.g. 와, 됐어! 'yes, it worked!') — same word, opposite feel, separated only by context and tone.

mistakes: Using bare 됐어 toward a server, elder, or boss.
Bare 됐어 is blunt 반말 and easily sounds annoyed ('forget it'). Upward, soften to 아니요, 괜찮아요, or at least 됐어요 / 됐습니다 with a friendly tone.
Treating 됐어요 as identical to 괜찮아요.
됐어요 is firmer and more final, and can imply mild impatience. For a gentle, frictionless 'no thanks', prefer 괜찮아요; save 됐어요 for when you need to be definite.
Confusing the refusal 됐어요 with the 'it worked!' 됐어요.
되다 also means 'to succeed/be done': 됐어! can mean 'it worked!'. Context and tone separate them; as a refusal it means 'that's enough', not 'success'.
